```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(targets)
library(hexbin)
library(ggrepel)
library(viridis)
library(patchwork)
library(ggnewscale)
library(igraph)
library(sf)
library(gridExtra)
library(grid)
library(knitr)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "svglite")

devtools::load_all(quiet = TRUE)
```

This is an attempt to build a basic AEP for algae with the information we have available. Although algae are data poor, they pose a number of advantages for this exercise:

1. Data poor species mean fewer difficult decisions to be made about lumping/splitting organisms
2. Algae can be assumed to be at the bottom of any food chains (this would be more relevant if copper were expected to biomagnify)
3. We only have information on one tissue type for algae (shoot tips), which means we don't need to build internal AEPs.

The process of this AEP will thus be conducted starting with the organism of interest. We will, for the time being, assume that the seaweed shoot tips (see below for species) are our TSE, and that they uptake copper exclusively from the marine water they grow in. We will then begin to back-fill the AEP to emissions data _based only on the data we have at this point_. Gap-filling will certainly be necessary, but we should discuss to what extent before committing.

# Request for comments

- In some cases only using data from above the Arctic circle means we don't have enough data; in other cases we have too much data. I propose to make this call based on data availability for a given case. Thoughts?
- The degree of investigation I've done on the datasets is fairly limited so far. In Peng et al (the microplastics AEP paper), they use geographically co-located sites. We can try and do this but it's not guaranteed that we will find such pairs. For the time being I've just used all sites above the Arctic Circle to represent conceptual fjords, algae, etc. Thoughts? 
- Likewise, I haven't spent much time looking at time trends so far. You can see some very messy linear modelling in the big summary plots for each matrix, to me they suggest nothing I would call a trend.
- To date, I haven't given all that much thought to flows between matrices. This is probably where the greatest amount of gap filling will be required. I am not sure how much focus to put here, though. It may be sufficient to, for example, mark a flow as well-quantified and understood because many papers/models exist, without having to investigate them in great detail.
- The current AEP diagrams are rather noisy and don't communicate the most important information well. I don't want to spend much time making them pretty at this stage, but thoughts on what the most important information to communicate is would be helpful
- The "EPEQ assessment" (basically WOE scoring) I've done for each node and edge isn't very appropriate for copper. I have some thoughts about how to adapt it, but what would you do?
- How important is it that AEPs are big and comprehensive versus small and modular? You can see for example that the AEP at the bottom includes a lot of sources (and could reasonably include more). The more boxes we put on the big diagram, the harder it is to work with and understand.

# Algae

```{r}
#| label: tbl-algae-setup
algae <- tar_read(load_literature_pqt) |>
  filter(SPECIES_GROUP == "Algae")

algae |>
  group_by(SAMPLE_SPECIES, REFERENCE_ID) |>
  reframe(n = n()) |>
  arrange(n) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

We have a lot of data for algae, but it's macroalgae rather than microalgae. We probably can't assume consistent internal concentrations across such a biodiverse set of taxa, but nevertheless it's a starting point. I can (and will) go looking for more papers, but I want to work with what I have first.

## Fucus vesiculosus

a.k.a Bladderwrack

Via Worms is found in [Arctic](https://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxdetails&id=145548#distributions) regions, but is it an arctic species?

## Ascophyllum nodosum

a.k.a Knotted wrack

Generally cosmopolitan distribution across the Atlantic. Cold tolerance uncertain, but probably sufficient for our purposes.

Note: Currently we just consider algae as whole organisms. Do we need to make a distinction between intracellular and extracellular stuff?

# Distribution of Copper Concentrations

There's one improbably high outlier in the dataset. We'll remove anything over 50mg/kg dry weight. Black Angel (2017) results are reported with SDs, while Vannmiljø data is just points. But, we need to be careful about sites, dates, and especially campaigns.

The below plot code uses the thresholds for coastal marine waters, since we don't have a background level for algae. We infer that seaweed bioaccumulate copper!

```{r}
#| label: make-algae-comparison
threshold_data <- generate_copper_thresholds() |>
  filter(ENVIRON_COMPARTMENT_SUB == "Marine/Salt Water")


algae_pointrange <- algae |>
  filter(MEASURED_VALUE <= 50) |>
  mutate(
    SITE_COMMENT = SITE_COMMENT |>
      str_remove("^.*?\\."),
    SITE_NAME = SITE_NAME |> str_remove("Vannmiljø Station")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = SITE_NAME, x = MEASURED_VALUE, colour = MEASURED_VALUE)) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = UNCERTAINTY_LOWER, xmax = UNCERTAINTY_UPPER)) +
  new_scale_color() +
  geom_vline(
    # TODO: Fix cvolours, add labels to lines.
    data = threshold_data,
    aes(xintercept = THRESHOLD_VALUE, color = TITLE_SHORT),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = str_wrap(SITE_COMMENT), x = UNCERTAINTY_UPPER + 0.5),
    colour = "black",
    hjust = 0
  ) +
  labs(y = "Site Code", x = "Measured Value (mg/kg)") +
  facet_wrap(
    facets = vars(MEASURED_UNIT_STANDARD),
    ncol = 1,
    scales = "free_y",
    space = "free_y"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Otherwise, our standard workup should be something like:

 - Any temporal patterns?
 - Any spatial patterns?
 - Any site selection rationale or nearby sources we might expect to drive elevated concentrations?

```{r}
#| label: make-algae-hexmaps
world_map <- map_data("world")
# reduce bbox size
get_study_area_bbox <- function() {
  st_bbox(c(xmin = -65, xmax = 40, ymin = 55, ymax = 75))
}

algae_hex <- algae |>
  filter(!is.na(LONGITUDE), !is.na(LATITUDE))

sample_size_map <- algae_hex |>
  ggplot(aes(x = LONGITUDE, y = LATITUDE)) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = world_map,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "grey95",
    colour = "grey80",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  stat_bin_hex(
    bins = 100,
    colour = NA
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "magma",
    trans = "sqrt",
    name = "Sample count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Sample Size",
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.title = element_blank()) +
  coord_fixed(
    ratio = 2,
    xlim = c(
      get_study_area_bbox()[[1]],
      get_study_area_bbox()[[3]]
    ),
    ylim = c(
      get_study_area_bbox()[[2]],
      get_study_area_bbox()[[4]]
    )
  )

mean_conc_map <- algae_hex |>
  ggplot(aes(x = LONGITUDE, y = LATITUDE, z = MEASURED_VALUE)) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = world_map,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "grey95",
    colour = "grey80",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  stat_summary_hex(
    fun = function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    bins = 100,
    colour = NA
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "viridis",
    name = "Mean concentration\n(mg/kg dry & wet)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.title = element_blank()) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean algae concentration by hexbin",
  ) +
  coord_fixed(
    ratio = 2,
    xlim = c(
      get_study_area_bbox()[[1]],
      get_study_area_bbox()[[3]]
    ),
    ylim = c(
      get_study_area_bbox()[[2]],
      get_study_area_bbox()[[4]]
    )
  )
```

Sample sizes are highest in the Oslofjord area, and concentrations are unusually high in mid-Norway (Tisler & Orkedalsfjorden). Why?

```{r}
#| label: fig-algae-overview
algae_timetrend <- algae |>
  filter(MEASURED_VALUE <= 50) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = SAMPLING_DATE, y = MEASURED_VALUE, group = SITE_NAME)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, aes(colour = SITE_NAME)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

algae_pointrange + (sample_size_map / mean_conc_map / algae_timetrend)
```

Well, that's helpful.

Can we be a bit more spatially intelligent without having to do lots more work?

```{r}
#| label: algae-site-cluster
# let's cluster our points based on proximity.
distance_matrix <- st_as_sf(algae, coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE")) |>
  st_set_crs(4326) |> # tell sf these are WGS84 lat/lon
  st_distance()

# for the sake of argument, sites within 20km of each other
# from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/77179007/group-spatial-points-by-distance-in-r-how-to-group-cluster-spatial-points-so-gr
binary_matrix <- matrix(
  as.numeric(
    distance_matrix
  ) <
    20000,
  nrow = nrow(distance_matrix)
)


g <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(binary_matrix)

# grouped algae sites
algae_grouped <- algae
algae_grouped$site_group <- factor(components(g)$membership)


# create sf (keep original lon/lat columns)
algae_sf <- st_as_sf(
  algae_grouped,
  coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
)

centroids <- algae_sf |>
  st_transform(3857) |> # metric projection for accurate centroids
  group_by(site_group) |>
  summarize(geometry = st_combine(geometry), .groups = "drop", n = n()) |> # combine points per group
  st_centroid() |> # centroid of multipoint
  st_transform(4326) # back to lon/lat (if needed)

# centroids is an sf point layer with site_group and geometry
centroids_xy <- centroids |>
  mutate(
    LONGITUDE = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 1],
    LATITUDE = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 2]
  )

groups_map <- ggplot(
  data = centroids_xy,
  aes(x = LONGITUDE, y = LATITUDE)
) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = world_map,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "grey95",
    colour = "grey80",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_label_repel(
    aes(colour = site_group, label = site_group),
    max.overlaps = 100
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +

  theme(legend.position = "none", axis.title = element_blank()) +
  coord_fixed(
    ratio = 2,
    xlim = c(
      get_study_area_bbox()[[1]],
      get_study_area_bbox()[[3]]
    ),
    ylim = c(
      get_study_area_bbox()[[2]],
      get_study_area_bbox()[[4]]
    )
  )

# strings to remove from comments:
remove_patterns <- c(
  # urls / emails / unicode quotes
  "(?i)https?://\\S+|www\\.\\S+|\\S+@\\S+",
  # parenthetical / bracket content
  "\\s*\\([^)]*\\)|\\s*\\[[^]]*\\]",
  # report codes like 01.01-385, 2021/09, 2290-12 etc.
  "\\b\\d{1,4}(?:[\\.\\-/]\\d{1,4})+\\b",
  # simple station / sample codes L1, L2, Stasjon 3, Station 4
  "\\bL\\d+\\b|\\bStasjon\\s*\\d+\\b|\\bStation\\s*\\d+\\b",
  # short code fragments like '01', '02' as standalone tokens (avoid years by requiring non-4-digit)
  "\\b(?!\\d{4}\\b)\\d{1,3}\\b",
  # report words (Norwegian / English) and common report prefixes
  "(?i)rapport(?:\\s+nr\\.?|nr\\.?|nummer|:)?.*?\\b|(?i)report(?:\\s+no\\.?|\\s+nr\\.?|\\s+nr)?",
  "(?i)rapporter?\\b|(?i)reference(?:\\s+site)?\\b|\\bref\\.?\\b",
  # vannmiljø / vm markers and resipient/resipientundersøkelse noise
  "(?i)vannmilj[oø]\\b|\\bvm\\b|(?i)resipient(?:unders[kq]økelse|unde)?",
  # 'Vm Emission ' and variants; Miljøgifter etc.
  "(?i)vm\\s*emission\\s*|(?i)miljøgifter\\b|(?i)miljøgifter\\s+i",
  # contractor / org names (common Norwegian consultancies + generic ' AS' suffix)
  "(?i)akvaplan-?niva|niva\\b|nina\\b|ramb[ao]ll\\b|norconsult\\b|asplan\\s+viak\\b|ngi\\b|ng\\&i\\b|APN|AS",
  "\\b\\p{Lu}[\\p{L}'’\\-]+(?:\\s+\\p{Lu}[\\p{L}'’\\-]+)*\\s+AS\\b",
  # page / folio / table refs
  "\\bpg?\\.?\\s*\\d+\\b|\\bp\\.\\s*\\d+\\b",
  # measurement / unit fragments that clutter comments
  "\\bmg/kg\\b|\\bmg/kg\\s*dry\\b|\\bmg/kg\\s*wet\\b|\\bSD\\b|\\bStandard\\s+Deviat(?:ion|ions)\\b",
  # stray punctuation sequences and repeated separators
  "[,;:\\|]{2,}|--+|\\.\\.+",
  # original comment
  "Original Comment:",
  "Emission :",
  "rsøkelse",
  "Vannmiljø Station",
  "Station"
)

# Some keywords for  characterisation:
# deponi
# industri*

# Example: combine and apply
combined <- str_c(remove_patterns, collapse = "|")
# then use: df |> mutate(SITE_COMMENT = str_remove_all(SITE_COMMENT, regex(combined, ignore_case=TRUE)) |> str_squish())

algae_sites_groups <- algae_grouped |>
  mutate(
    SITE_COMMENT = str_remove_all(
      SITE_COMMENT,
      regex(combined, ignore_case = TRUE)
    ) |>
      str_squish(),
    SITE_NAME = str_remove_all(
      SITE_NAME,
      regex(combined, ignore_case = TRUE)
    ) |>
      str_squish()
  ) |>
  reframe(
    .by = "site_group",
    condensed_name = paste(unique(SITE_NAME), collapse = ";"),
    condensed_comments = paste(unique(SITE_COMMENT), collapse = ";"),
    condensed_site_types = paste(
      unique(SITE_GEOGRAPHIC_FEATURE),
      collapse = ";"
    ),
    condensed_site_subtypes = paste(
      unique(SITE_GEOGRAPHIC_FEATURE_SUB),
      collapse = ";"
    ),
    site_characterisation = case_when(
      str_detect(condensed_comments, "(?i)ndustr") ~ "Industrial",
      .default = NA_character_
    ),
    n_sites = n(),
    n_samples = sum(MEASURED_N)
  )


groups_map
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-alge-groups
algae_sites_groups |>
  select(-condensed_comments) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

There's one improbably high outlier in the dataset. We'll remove anything over 50mg/kg dry weight. Black Angel (2017) results are reported with SDs, while Vannmiljø data is just points. But, we need to be careful about sites, dates, and especially campaigns.

The below plot code uses the thresholds for coastal marine waters, since we don't have a background level for algae. We infer that seaweed bioaccumulate copper!

Sample sizes are highest in the Oslofjord area, and concentrations are unusually high in mid-Norway (Tisler & Orkedalsfjorden). Why?

# EPEQ Assessment

We have a fairly disordered dataset here, but rather than wait for the perfect one we will attempt to do the assessment (badly) so we can continue to build the network. Based on Peng et al., for each node (and edge) we want to know how essential, plausible, evidence-based (or empirical) and quantified (understood mechanistically and quantitatively) it is. 

These criteria make a lot of sense for AOPs and anthropogenic pollutants (like microplastics), but are somewhat less informative for an essential trace nutrient and key ingredient of the earth's core.

![Alt text](../images/peng_aep_diagram.png)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-epeq-assessment-algae
# just based on wet weights right now
algae_wet_weight <- algae |> filter(MEASURED_UNIT_STANDARD == "mg/kg (wet)")

# mean +- SD
algae_mean <- algae_wet_weight |>
  reframe(mean_value = mean(MEASURED_VALUE_STANDARD, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull()
algae_sd <- algae_wet_weight |>
  reframe(sd_value = sd(MEASURED_VALUE_STANDARD, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull()
# sample size
algae_n = algae_wet_weight |> reframe(n = n()) |> pull()
# lines of evidence
# counting Vm as one feels wrong, but what can you do?
algae_lines_of_evidence <- algae_wet_weight |>
  reframe(.by = REFERENCE_ID) |>
  nrow()
# Essentiality (1-3)
algae_essentiality_score = 3
algae_essentiality_justification = "Copper is an essential component in photosynthesis (?). Thus algae must have a system for the controlled uptake of copper."
# Plausibility (1-3)
algae_plausibility_score = 3
algae_plausibility_justification = "As above, the role of copper in photosynthetic organisms (including algae) is well studied and understood."
# Evidence (1-3)
algae_evidence_score = 3
algae_evidence_justification = "Although the studied dataset contains limited evidence on copper concentrations in algae, measured concentrations are well in excess of background water concentrations. Strong specific evidence is not considered necessarily in light of the overall scientific consensus."
# Quantification (1-3)
algae_quantification_score = 2
algae_quantification_justification = "Copper kinetics and metabolism in algae are assumed to be well understood, although such literature was not included in the study criteria."

# Plus justifications

# so our evidence is shaped like (for nodes)
# build long EPEQ table for algae
epeq_algae_long <- tibble(
  parameter = c(
    "matrix",
    "mean",
    "sd",
    "n",
    "n_lines_of_evidence",
    "essentiality_score",
    "plausibility_score",
    "evidence_score",
    "quantification_score"
  ),
  value = c(
    "Biota (Aquatic) - Seaweed - Shoot Tips",
    as.character(algae_mean),
    as.character(algae_sd),
    as.character(algae_n),
    as.character(algae_lines_of_evidence),
    as.character(algae_essentiality_score),
    as.character(algae_plausibility_score),
    as.character(algae_evidence_score),
    as.character(algae_quantification_score)
  ),
  justification = c(
    NA_character_,
    NA_character_,
    NA_character_,
    NA_character_,
    NA_character_,
    algae_essentiality_justification,
    algae_plausibility_justification,
    algae_evidence_justification,
    algae_quantification_justification
  )
) |>
  as_tibble()

epeq_algae_long |>
  knitr::kable()
```

# Marine Water

Obviously there's going to be loads of this. Some important questions: 1. Is there actually any significant difference between fjords, estuaries, near and far ocean? (*some* fjords are likely to be quite contaminated, but will that show up in our data?)

In fact, our data is (currently) all fjords, because Vannmiljø doesn't monitor open ocean (as far as I know... but what about O&G monitoring?)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-marine-setup
marine <- tar_read(load_literature_pqt) |>
  filter(ENVIRON_COMPARTMENT_SUB == "Marine/Salt Water", LATITUDE >= 66.5)

marine |>
  group_by(
    SITE_GEOGRAPHIC_FEATURE,
    SITE_GEOGRAPHIC_FEATURE_SUB,
    REFERENCE_ID
  ) |>
  reframe(n = n()) |>
  arrange(n) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Marine water gets the same analysis as algae, although it's likely to be more complicated due to the greater amount of data. We won't show the full comments here, we simply don't have the space.

```{r}
    aes(label = str_wrap(SITE_COMMENT), x = UNCERTAINTY_UPPER + 0.5),
    colour = "black",
    hjust = 0
  ) +
  labs(y = "Site Code", x = "Measured Value (mg/L)") +
  facet_wrap(
    facets = vars(MEASURED_UNIT_STANDARD),
    ncol = 1,
    scales = "free_y",
    space = "free_y"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

We have a handful of sites in Nordfjorden with elevated copper concentrations (\>5 mg/L), but most are in the background-Level II zone. It's probably safe to just take an average here, although it would be wise to drill down further spatially - but do we have the time to do that for each set of sites?

# EPEQ Assessment

We can do the same assessment with the marine data; again, it's not going to be great.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-epeq_assessment-marine
# mean +- SD
marine_mean <- marine |>
  reframe(mean_value = mean(MEASURED_VALUE_STANDARD, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull()
marine_sd <- marine |>
  reframe(sd_value = sd(MEASURED_VALUE_STANDARD, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull()
# sample size
marine_n = marine |> reframe(n = n()) |> pull()
# lines of evidence
# counting Vm as one feels wrong, but what can you do?
marine_lines_of_evidence <- marine |>
  reframe(.by = REFERENCE_ID) |>
  nrow()
# Essentiality (1-3)
marine_essentiality_score = 3
marine_essentiality_justification = "Copper is known to be naturally present in the earth's crust and aquatic ecosystems."
# Plausibility (1-3)
marine_plausibility_score = 3
marine_plausibility_justification = "As above."
# Evidence (1-3)
marine_evidence_score = 3
marine_evidence_justification = "The studied dataset contains substantial evidence on copper concentrations in marine water."
# Quantification (1-3)
marine_quantification_score = 2
marine_quantification_justification = "Copper kinetics in marine environments are generally well studied and modelled. I can perhaps cite some papers here, but I'll have to get them via gap-filling."
# TODO: could add CREED here as a measure of data quality?

# so our evidence is shaped like (for nodes)
# build long EPEQ table for marine
epeq_marine_long <- tibble(
  parameter = c(
    "matrix",
    "mean",
    "sd",
    # TODO: add unit
    "n",
    "n_lines_of_evidence",
    "essentiality_score",
    "plausibility_score",
    "evidence_score",
    "quantification_score"
  ),
  value = c(
    "Aquatic (Marine/Sea Water)",
    as.character(marine_mean),
    as.character(marine_sd),
    as.character(marine_n),
    as.character(marine_lines_of_evidence),
    as.character(marine_essentiality_score),
    as.character(marine_plausibility_score),
    as.character(marine_evidence_score),
    as.character(marine_quantification_score)
  ),
  justification = c(
    NA_character_,
    NA_character_,
    NA_character_,
    NA_character_,
    NA_character_,
    marine_essentiality_justification,
    marine_plausibility_justification,
    marine_evidence_justification,
    marine_quantification_justification
  )
) |>
  as_tibble()

epeq_marine_long |>
  knitr::kable()
```

# Freshwater - Rivers/Streams/Canals

Next node we might expect is rivers as a source of copper. This is also a little tricky, because source characterisation for a long river is even harder (and we might generally expect them to be less homogeneous than the ocean as a consequence of their hydrology). But we can try.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-freshwater-setup
freshwater <- tar_read(load_literature_pqt) |>
  filter(
    ENVIRON_COMPARTMENT_SUB == "Freshwater",
    LATITUDE >= 66.5,
    SITE_GEOGRAPHIC_FEATURE == "River, stream, canal"
  )

freshwater |>
  group_by(
    SITE_GEOGRAPHIC_FEATURE,
    SITE_GEOGRAPHIC_FEATURE_SUB,
    REFERENCE_ID
  ) |>
  reframe(n = n()) |>
  arrange(n) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

We have lots of data for rivers/streams above the arctic circle, and some of it has super-high concentrations.

```{r}
#| label: freshwater-cluster
distance_matrix <- st_as_sf(freshwater, coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE")) |>
  st_set_crs(4326) |> # tell sf these are WGS84 lat/lon
  st_distance()

binary_matrix <- matrix(
  as.numeric(
    distance_matrix
  ) <
    20000,
  nrow = nrow(distance_matrix)
)

g <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(binary_matrix)

# grouped freshwater sites
freshwater_grouped <- freshwater
freshwater_grouped$site_group <- factor(components(g)$membership)


# create sf (keep original lon/lat columns)
freshwater_sf <- st_as_sf(
  freshwater_grouped,
  coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
)

centroids <- freshwater_sf |>
  st_transform(3857) |> # metric projection for accurate centroids
  group_by(site_group) |>
  summarize(geometry = st_combine(geometry), .groups = "drop", n = n()) |> # combine points per group
  st_centroid() |> # centroid of multipoint
  st_transform(4326) # back to lon/lat (if needed)

# centroids is an sf point layer with site_group and geometry
centroids_xy <- centroids |>
  mutate(
    LONGITUDE = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 1],
    LATITUDE = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 2]
  )

groups_map <- ggplot(
  data = centroids_xy,
  aes(x = LONGITUDE, y = LATITUDE)
) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = world_map,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "grey95",
    colour = "grey80",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_label_repel(
    aes(colour = site_group, label = site_group),
    max.overlaps = 100
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +

  theme(legend.position = "none", axis.title = element_blank()) +
  coord_fixed(
    ratio = 2,
    xlim = c(
      get_study_area_bbox()[[1]],
      get_study_area_bbox()[[3]]
    ),
    ylim = c(
      get_study_area_bbox()[[2]],
      get_study_area_bbox()[[4]]
    )
  )

# Example: combine and apply
combined <- str_c(remove_patterns, collapse = "|")

freshwater_sites_groups <- freshwater_grouped |>
  mutate(
    SITE_COMMENT = str_remove_all(
      SITE_COMMENT,
      regex(combined, ignore_case = TRUE)
    ) |>
      str_squish(),
    SITE_NAME = str_remove_all(
      SITE_NAME,
      regex(combined, ignore_case = TRUE)
    ) |>
      str_squish()
  ) |>
  reframe(
    .by = "site_group",
    condensed_name = paste(unique(SITE_NAME), collapse = ";"),
    condensed_comments = paste(unique(SITE_COMMENT), collapse = ";"),
    condensed_site_types = paste(
      unique(SITE_GEOGRAPHIC_FEATURE),
      collapse = ";"
    ),
    condensed_site_subtypes = paste(
      unique(SITE_GEOGRAPHIC_FEATURE_SUB),
      collapse = ";"
    ),
    site_characterisation = case_when(
      str_detect(condensed_comments, "(?i)ndustr") ~ "Industrial",
      .default = NA_character_
    ),
    n_sites = n(),
    n_samples = sum(MEASURED_N)
  )

groups_map
```

# Gap-Filling

Initial research suggests it's difficult to say how much copper is "in algae". We can still do AEP stuff, but the evidence is necessarily going to be weak. Some key points:

- Copper is also a stressor and essential nutrient in microalgae, but knowledge is spotty https://www.mdpi.com/2305-6304/10/9/527

I guess we can start with the information we have and hopefull extend it if/when we get some more data...

# Edges

So far we've just done nodes, which is easy. Edges are harder. We hypothesise the following flows:

- Marine Water -\> Algae
- Freshwater -\> Marine Water
- Atmosphere -\> Marine Water
- Atmosphere -\> Fresh Water
- Atmosphere -\> Soil
- Soil -\> Fresh Water

Here's the two most important ones:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-flows-epeq
flows_epeq <- tribble(
  ~flow_name                                    , ~from               , ~to                    , ~magnitude , ~unit , ~n , ~sd , ~essentiality_score , ~essentiality_justification     , ~plausibility_score , ~plausibility_justification                                 , ~evidence_score , ~evidence_justification                           , ~quantification_score , ~quantification_justification                        , ~comments                                                                                                                                                         ,
  "Algal Uptake"                                , "Marine/Salt Water" , "Algae Whole Organism" , NA         , NA    , NA , NA  ,                   3 , "it's got to get there somehow" ,                   3 , "cu is a micronutrient and thus must be controlled somehow" ,               1 , "evidence exists but I haven't gapfilled it yet." ,                     1 , "evidence may exist but I haven't gap-filled it yet" , "Copper uptake by organisms is known to be active regulated. A simple magnitude of uptake (e.g. BCF) is unlikely to capture the relationship in a meaningul way." ,
  "Riverine Copper Inputs to Marine/Salt Water" , "Freshwater"        , "Marine/Salt Water"    , NA         , NA    , NA , NA  ,                   3 , "rivers aren't the only input"  ,                   3 , "rivers carry crust material towards the sea"               ,               1 , "evidence exists but I haven't gapfilled it yet." ,                     1 , "evidence may exist but I haven't gap-filled it yet" , "This is also tricky to represnt just as a simple node, but I think Comber et al has some estimates in terms of kg/year we can use."
)

flows_epeq |>
  knitr::kable()
```
